quotedTweet.text:
Why is oil price not simply Brent?

Not so long ago, people used the word 'oil prices' loosely to describe everything from crude oil to diesel to gasoline. That wasn't necessarily wrong either since the prices tracked each other closely.

Slowly, refining capacity in the world declined. Some mega refineries got built in the Middle East, China and Africa, while the smaller, older outfits were rationalized, many in the Atlantic Basin. 

Then came the US-Iran war. Middle Eastern refineries suffered strikes and could not resume normal operations quickly. Asian refineries suffered loss of feedstock due to the Strait of Hormuz closure but eventually diversified their crude slate to run up to max. However refineries in China were curtailed in production by government-mandated product export quotas.

The crisis further compounded when Ukraine started attacking Russian refineries relentless with drones. 

All these resulted in refining capacity shortages. When refining is constrained, it results in a blowout of product cracks, which is the spread between product and crude. Lo and behold, 'oil prices' cannot be used interchangeably anymore and we have to differentiate between crude oil (Brent) and diesel or mogas prices.

So if we see flatprice coming off, we are not necessarily going to see diesel or gasoline prices coming off in the same way in the current environment we are in. Refining capacity is expected to remain constrained until either Russia, China and/or the Middle Eastern refineries start running again at higher throughput, or demand destruction happens in a large scale.

And don't forget that exorbitant freight rate plaguing the markets which increases the price of crude delivered into the refineries. The product prices will need to factor in the entire cost of input, not just flatprice!

Until then, be more explicit with which 'oil price' you are referring to. We are far from the good old days.

#oott

quotedTweet.text:
Crude refining margin 101

The price of crude delivered to refinery = Benchmark + FOB premium + freight cost

Benchmark can be ICE Brent, Dated Brent, Nymex WTI or Dubai.

FOB premium is a factor of supply and demand, quality of crude and logistics. If that crude is red hot in demand, FOB goes up. FOB premium is also known as cash diff/differential.

Freight cost has its own supply and demand angle. Right now VLCCs are in short supply due to highly inefficient logistics caused by the war, hence the crazy valuations there.

Crude margins is then the value of the crude minus the delivered price of crude. The value of the crude is also known as gross product worth (GPW). You multiply product cracks with the yields obtained from the crude.

Each refinery values the crude differently due to unique refining configurations. They run Linear Programming (LPs) to obtain these valuations.

In the current climate, refining margin must be ≥0 since refining is short. If it goes below 0, then something in the equation needs to adjust. I.e. either FOB  premium or freight goes down, or product cracks rise. 

In Sparta, we model all of the above and align 90 crudes to the same delivery window for 8 refining destinations with 3 different refining configurations per region.

Hope this explains the basics of crude refining economics.

#oott

Note published to @SpartaCommo clients last evening, do subscribe if you have not already:

Saudi E/W pipeline outage update
13 Sep 26 - 15:00 CEST

1⃣ According to the Ministry of Energy, the Saudi East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Madinah regions was subjected to multiple attacks on Thursday 10 September. The pipeline has been shutdown as a precautionary measure. This pipeline typically carries Arab Light and Arab Heavy crude, both to domestic refineries and to the export markets.

2⃣ Duration of the outage is unknown. The attacks apparently came from Iraq, and not directly related to the Houthis that had seized the port city of Mocha on Thursday.

3⃣ If the pipelines flows are restored within a short time, there should have enough buffer within the system to keep the domestic refineries running. However exports of crude via the Red Sea will be met with some difficulty after drawing down from tank inventories at Yanbu.

4⃣ Additionally production shut-ins are likely if the crude stocks hits tank top on the Eastern side of Saudi. We anticipate dirty freight availability to be the key constraint in managing the evacuation option ex Ras Tanura. This will support TD3c markets further.

5⃣ European refiners (particularly in the Med) that have been relying on Saudi crude ex Sidi Kerir will also face temporary prompt shortages. This will mirror how Asian refineries reacted at the onset of the SoH closure, whereby reducing runrates is the likely outcome while waiting for viable crude replacements to arrive.

6⃣ Eastern refiners are not fully spared from this scenario as well since Korea and Japan have been seen chartering cargoes ex-Sidi Kerir but at least they may still benefit from getting crude ex Gulf of Oman in a shorter time if Saudi is able to offer this option.

7⃣ 400 kbd YASREF refinery, 400 kbd SAMREF and 245 kbd Yanbu refinery exports products, mainly distillates. If the pipeline outage exceeds the time the refineries have on available crude buffers, then the refineries may be forced to shutdown later due to crude unavailability. This is the likely worst case scenario which will only happen if the pipeline is out for an extended period of time.

8⃣ This means the diesel tightness we have seen in Europe will become further exacerbated with some Med refineries turning down on intake in the prompt while reevaluating crude replacement options, and potentially facing the worst-case scenario of the Saudi refineries themselves not exporting products.

9⃣ Thus we are likely going to see higher flatprice, Brent-Dubai EFS, DFL, prompt crude timespreads, crude FOB diffs, diesel timespreads and even stronger cracks when we start the week, until further clarity is found. This is of course subject to any new headlines of peace deals that can quickly temper the excitement.

🔟 Jet and mogas cracks will likely be pulled up by the diesel strength. Dirty freight could also move up with more inefficient freight routings anticipated.

An extended outage could also see IEA coming in with further SPR release to calm the markets, but that buffer is getting thinner.

EUROPE's gas storage starts (tentatively) to improve

Europe’s gas storage remains critically low but there are tentative signs of improvement after prices rose to the highest for almost four years, forcing reductions in consumption and attracting more LNG away from other regions. 

The summer refill season ended with storage sites on average less than 72% full on September 30, down from 83% on the same date last year, and an average of more than 88% over the last decade. 

Storage rates across the European Union were the lowest for the time of year in records stretching back to 2011, according to data compiled by Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).  

Storage will continue to increase for several more weeks until late October or even early November but late additions are likely to be smaller as temperatures fall and heating demand increases ...

When they "release" they drop that mandated holding level, but they don't *actually* sell the barrels themselves.

Presumably currently very steep backwardation will be enough of an incentive for commercial stockholders to actually sell them, but it's not a guarantee.

COT on #commodities: Managed money remained firmly on the defensive in the week to 29 September as a stronger dollar and surging US Treasury yields helped drive the Bloomberg Commodity Index down 2.1%.
Funds sold 18 of 25 major commodity futures, led by crude oil, natural gas, gold, silver, soybeans and corn. The combined WTI and Brent net long fell 31k contracts to a five-week low.
Gold continues to highlight a notable divergence: hedge funds cut 2.7 million ounces of exposure during September, while ETF investors added 1.7 million ounces, lifting holdings to a four-year high.
Agriculture positioning remains relatively sticky, with a 6% price decline since early September triggering only an 11% reduction in the record net long.
More in my Monday update.

The latest COT forex update covers the week to 29 September, when an accelerating sell-off in US Treasuries saw the 10-year yield jump 27 basis points to 5.24%, underpinning the dollar, which gained around 1% against a broad basket of major peers.
For a second consecutive week, these developments triggered a significant shift in speculative FX positioning as traders rushed back into dollar longs. The aggregate dollar long against eight IMM currency futures jumped 39% to USD 25.3 billion, a four-week high and up sharply from just USD 6 billion two weeks earlier.
largest shifts were seen against CAD, EUR, JPY and AUD. Beyond the yen, the only other remaining net long was in MXN, where bullish exposure was cut by 30% to a 14-month low. https://t.co/XEuN96dnSv

Container freight: The Drewry World Container Index recorded a second consecutive weekly decline, but the headline masks an unusually wide divergence between major trade routes. Shanghai–Los Angeles and Shanghai–New York rates are both up around 216% YTD, trading at +4-year highs, while Shanghai–Rotterdam is up just 32% and Shanghai–Genoa only 8%.

The gap largely reflects different capacity dynamics. On the Transpacific, resilient US-bound demand has coincided with aggressive capacity management by carriers through blank sailings, while congestion at major Asian ports has further constrained effective capacity. Drewry currently puts Shanghai–LA at USD 7,835 per 40-foot container and Shanghai–NY at USD 10,428. DrewryEurope is moving in the opposite direction. Shanghai–Rotterdam and Shanghai–Genoa rates have fallen for 12 consecutive weeks, reflecting softer demand and, importantly, the gradual return of vessels through the Suez Canal. Suez transits in week 39 were 68% above year-ago levels, shortening voyages and effectively releasing additional vessel capacity onto Asia–Europe routes. 

The result is a highly bifurcated container market: US-bound freight remains expensive primarily because effective capacity is being kept tight, while Europe is increasingly feeling the deflationary impact of returning capacity and weaker demand. With China's Golden Week now underway, Drewry expects some near-term easing on both routes, but the sizeable Transpacific premium may persist unless carriers restore capacity more aggressively.

Broad commodity losses mask persistent supply risks. Recovering crude flows offer relief, but fuel shortages, tight copper availability and El Niño risks remain. Gold ETF demand holds up despite price weakness.

#Agriculture: The @UNFAO Food Price Index averaged 136 points in September, reaching a 4½-year high and rising 5.8% year-on-year. The increase was driven primarily by strong gains in sugar (+6.1%) and cereals (+5.1%), with vegetable oils (+0.9%) also contributing. Meat prices (-1.1%) were the only major component to decline last month, while dairy prices were broadly unchanged.

Highlights from the report: 
The FAO Cereal Price Index rose sharply in September, driven by tightening supply and growing logistical risks. Wheat prices were supported by Black Sea export constraints, which pushed buyers towards alternative origins, as well as dry weather ahead of North American winter wheat planting. Maize also strengthened as disappointing US yields, reduced Brazilian export availability and Black Sea disruptions tightened the supply outlook. Elevated fuel, fertiliser and freight costs linked to uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz added further support, particularly for crops with biofuel exposure. Rice prices edged higher on weather concerns and seasonally tighter supplies.

The FAO Vegetable Oil Price Index rose modestly, led by palm oil, where strong import demand and concerns about dry weather affecting Southeast Asian production outweighed weakness elsewhere. Sunflower oil declined on expectations of ample Black Sea supplies, although logistical constraints limited the downside. Soy oil remained supported by robust biofuel demand.

The FAO Meat Price Index declined as ample supplies weighed on poultry and pork. Brazilian poultry exports faced softer EU demand following new import requirements, while increased pig meat availability across major producing regions pressured prices. Beef and sheep meat prices were broadly stable, with regional differences reflecting shifts in demand, trade policy and currency movements.

The FAO Dairy Price Index was broadly unchanged. Strong Asian demand and limited prompt availability supported milk powder prices, while cheese weakened amid softer European demand, strong US export competition and rising seasonal supply from Oceania. Butter was little changed, with tighter European milkfat availability offsetting weaker prices elsewhere.

The FAO Sugar Price Index rose strongly as the market priced a tighter global supply outlook. Smaller EU beet acreage and adverse weather, weaker production prospects in Thailand, concerns about India's crop amid below-normal rainfall and developing El Niño conditions, and harvest disruptions caused by heavy rain in Brazil all contributed to the increase.

The energy complex trades lower, led by gasoil (-4.7%) and ULSD (-3.3%), as the US pressures France and Germany to release emergency diesel stocks or potentially face a US diesel export ban. France has reportedly proposed releasing 50 million barrels of European diesel and 50 million barrels of crude across IEA members, conditional on Washington refraining from unilateral export restrictions, with G7 leaders potentially discussing next steps later today (Reuters).

The developments once again highlight that the main stress in energy markets has shifted from crude availability to refined products. Middle East crude flows are recovering, but reduced refinery capacity and output across the Middle East and Russia, together with China cancelling oil-product export cargoes to bolster domestic supply, continue to constrain global fuel availability and keep prices elevated.

The Bloomberg chart shows gasoil (white) and ULSD (blue) priced in USD per barrel both falling to one-month lows on this development.

RBOB gasoline leads this week’s performance table, up 5.8%, after the EIA reported a further decline in nationwide inventories to their lowest since November 2014. Distillate stocks also fell to their lowest seasonal level on record, with product tightness partly reflecting a seasonal and temporary drop in refinery activity, as crude runs fell by 1 mb/d to a five-month low. Meanwhile, US crude exports slowed to 3.6 mb/d as more Middle Eastern barrels were heading for the global market, while domestic production climbed to another record at 13.96 mb/d.
